big: A gilt fund with a duration of 6 slipped 3% in one month when yields rose by half a percent. One number on the factsheet had already told us how hard it would be hit.

lines: What does a duration of 6 years mean for my money? My gilt fund's NAV moved a lot last month.
It is a rate-sensitivity number. It is not a lock-in. Watch the same 1% rate move hit two funds.

rows: On ₹10 lakh, the move is about (₹ thousand)
alt: Bars comparing a fund of duration 2 and one of duration 6 for a 1% change in yields
caps: Two funds with ₹10 lakh each. Fund A has a modified duration of 2. Fund B has 6.
Yields rise 1%. Price change is about duration × 1%, so A falls about 2% and B about 6%.
If yields fall 1%, the same sizes work in reverse: A gains about 2%, B about 6%.
On ₹10 lakh, that is about ₹20,000 against ₹60,000.
Longer duration means more rate risk, and more reward if rates fall.

alt: Three lines for funds of duration 2, 5 and 8 through a made-up path of yields
caps: A made-up decade. Yields start at 7%, jump to 9% by year 3, then drift down to 6%.
Duration 8 takes the hit, about 9% down at year 3. Duration 2 keeps on earning.
As yields fall, the longer fund gains the most.
The deepest falls: none, about 3% and about 9%. Longer duration, bigger swings.
Each year is the starting yield minus duration × the change in yield. A guide, not a promise.

intro: Four numbers on a gilt fund's factsheet. Only one of them tells you the price move for a 1% change in yields.
note: Modified duration is Macaulay duration divided by (1 + yield): 5.9 ÷ 1.074 = 5.5. Use it to estimate the price move.

q: Meena holds ₹20 lakh in a gilt fund with a modified duration of 6. Yields rise by 0.5% this month. About how much does the price effect take off her holding?
opts: Nothing, because a month of coupons covers it
why: That is the effect of a full 1% rise. Her fund saw a rise of 0.5%, so the hit is half of that.
That is just the change in yield applied to her money. Duration multiplies it, and here the multiplier is 6.
Price change is about duration × change in yield, so 6 × 0.5% is 3%, and 3% of ₹20 lakh is ₹60,000.
A month of coupons adds only about 0.6% of value for a 7% portfolio. That is far less than a 3% price drop.

q: Meena says a duration of 6 years means her money is locked for six years. What is the sound reply?
opts: It means the fund cannot repay her before six years are over
No lock-in: it shows price sensitivity, and she can redeem any day
It means every bond in the fund matures exactly six years from now
It means the fund loses 6% each year until the six years pass
why: No lock-in exists in an open-ended debt fund. Duration is a sensitivity measure, not a repayment date.
Duration estimates how much the price moves for a 1% change in yields. Open-ended funds can be redeemed on any business day.
The portfolio holds many bonds with different maturities. Duration is a weighted average figure, not one date.
A fund does not lose a fixed 6% a year. Duration scales a move in yields, which can be up or down.

q: A factsheet shows average maturity 8.2 years, Macaulay duration 5.9, modified duration 5.5 and YTM 7.4%. For a quick estimate of the price hit from a 1% rise in yields, which figure does the adviser use?
why: Average maturity ignores when the coupons arrive. It overstates sensitivity because coupons shorten the true timing.
Macaulay duration is a weighted time to get your cash back. Divide by (1 + yield) to get the price sensitivity.
Modified duration is Macaulay ÷ (1 + yield), which is 5.9 ÷ 1.074 = 5.5. It links price moves to yield moves directly.
YTM is an expected annual return. It says what the portfolio earns, not how far the price moves when yields do.

q: A 10-year 7% bond at ₹1,000 has a modified duration of 7.02. Yields rise from 7% to 8%. Which estimate of the new price is best?
opts: About ₹1,070, because a higher yield means a higher price
About ₹993, since a 1% rise cuts only about 0.7% of the price
About ₹70, because that is the coupon the bond pays
why: Higher yields push prices down, not up. Price and yield move in opposite directions.
The 0.7% reading mixes up the decimal. With a duration of 7.02, a 1% rise cuts about 7% of the price, not 0.7%.
₹70 is the yearly coupon, and it is not a price. The price estimate is ₹1,000 less about ₹70, which is about ₹930.
7.02 × 1% is about 7%, or ₹70, off ₹1,000. Duration is a straight-line guide, so the exact price of ₹933 differs slightly.

pts: Price change ≈ -modified duration × change in yield.
Duration is rate risk, not a lock-in: longer duration swings more, both ways.
Find modified duration on the factsheet. It is not the same as average maturity.
